name: Kannayiranathar Temple, Tirukkaravasal
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung in the Tevaram
summary: Tirukkaravasal, also called Tirukarayil, near Tiruvarur, honours Shiva as Kannayiranathar, 'the lord of a thousand eyes.' A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Sambandar and Appar, it is rich in sacred tanks and legends: King Muchukunda is said to have worshipped an emerald lingam given by Indra, Brahma was freed from a curse in its waters, and the serpent Adisesha regained his sight here — so the temple's theerthams are revered as healing waters, especially for ailments of the eyes.

sections.history: Tirukkaravasal, whose older name is Tirukarayil, is an ancient Shaiva site near Tiruvarur, revered in the seventh-century Tevaram and listed among the Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Kaveri's southern bank — by Dinamalar's reckoning the 119th such shrine, sung by Sambandar and Appar. The stone temple belongs to the Chola period, around the ninth century, with later renovation. Sources place it variously in Tiruvarur and Nagapattinam districts, reflecting the shifting of modern administrative lines across the old delta country.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Kannayiranathar. It is especially rich in sacred tanks: the Brahma Teertham, tied to Brahma's release from a curse, and the Sesha Teertham, linked to the serpent Adisesha, whose waters are believed to cure diseases of the eyes and skin. A Vinayaka shrine, Kadukkai Vinayakar, preserves its own curious tale. The temple's many tirthas make it as much a place of sacred waters as of stone.
sections.legends: Several legends gather at Tirukkaravasal. King Muchukunda is said to have worshipped here an emerald lingam granted to him by Indra. Brahma is said to have bathed in the temple tank to be freed from a curse, and the Sesha Teertham is traced to Adisesha, the cosmic serpent, who regained his sight in its waters — which is why pilgrims seek them for ailments of the eyes. The Kadukkai Vinayakar shrine recalls a merchant whose cartload of nutmeg is said to have turned to kadukkai (myrobalan) at the lord's will.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi observances and the annual Brahmotsavam. The healing reputation of its waters draws a steady stream of pilgrims seeking relief, especially for the eyes, and ritual bathing in the tanks is a central act of worship here.
sections.experience: Tirukkaravasal is a temple of sacred waters as much as of darshan. Pilgrims come to bathe in the Brahma and Sesha tanks and to pray before Kannayiranathar, the lord of a thousand eyes, with special hope for the healing of sight. The layered legends of king, creator and cosmic serpent give the quiet delta shrine a sense of depth beyond its modest scale.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukkaravasal is near Tiruvarur (some sources list Nagapattinam district), roughly 15-18 km from Tiruvarur; the nearest rail heads are Tiruvarur and Nagapattinam, with local buses and taxis to the village.
